subject: ela
skillName: Identify different story points of view

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The city was putting in a new bike lane on Maple Street. Mr. Hassan, who drove his delivery truck down Maple Street every day, shook his head. "They're taking away a lane of traffic. My route will take twice as long." Twelve-year-old Cleo, who biked to school every day, read the news and pumped her fist. "Finally! I've almost been hit three times this year."

Explain BOTH characters' points of view on the new bike lane. Then explain why their backgrounds lead them to see the same change so differently.
items.answer: Mr. Hassan sees the bike lane as a problem because it removes a traffic lane he depends on for his job. He measures the change by its effect on his delivery time. Cleo sees the bike lane as a life-saving improvement. She has nearly been hit by cars three times, so the bike lane directly protects her. Their backgrounds lead to opposite views: Mr. Hassan is a driver whose efficiency is hurt, while Cleo is a cyclist whose safety has been at risk. Same change, different stakes.

steps: Mr. Hassan's point of view: The bike lane takes away road space he needs for deliveries, slowing him down.
Evidence for Mr. Hassan: 'They're taking away a lane of traffic. My route will take twice as long.'
Cleo's point of view: The bike lane is a safety measure that protects cyclists like her.
Evidence for Cleo: She has 'almost been hit three times this year' — the lane addresses a real danger she faces.
Why they differ: Mr. Hassan's job depends on traffic flow; Cleo's safety depends on road separation.
Same change affects each character's most important concern in opposite ways.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The school was going to cut the art program to make room for more test-prep classes. Ms. Rivera, the art teacher, was heartbroken. "Art is how many students find their voice," she said. Principal Banks said he understood, but explained, "Test scores determine our school's funding. Without better scores, we may not have any programs at all."

Explain both Ms. Rivera's and Principal Banks's points of view. Why does each believe what they do? Use specific evidence from the story.
items.answer: Ms. Rivera believes art is essential because it gives students a way to express themselves. She feels the cut is harmful to students who rely on art to communicate and thrive. Principal Banks also cares about students, but his point of view is practical: test scores control the school's funding, and without money, there will be no programs at all. He is not against art, but he sees survival as the priority. Both characters want the best for students, but they define 'best' very differently based on what each person knows and is responsible for.

steps: Ms. Rivera's point of view: Art is a critical outlet for students, and cutting it harms their development.
Evidence: 'Art is how many students find their voice' — she sees deep personal value in the program.
Principal Banks's point of view: Test scores fund the school; without them, all programs disappear.
Evidence: 'Without better scores, we may not have any programs at all' — he sees a larger institutional risk.
Why they differ: Ms. Rivera measures impact by student growth; Banks measures it by financial survival.
Both care about students but see the problem from opposite angles of their roles.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Sofia grew up in a small town. When her family moved to the city, her mother said, "I love the energy here — restaurants open at midnight, buses running all night, people from everywhere!" Sofia lay awake listening to sirens and car horns. "I can't sleep," she whispered. "Everything is too loud and too fast."

Explain Sofia's point of view and her mother's point of view about city life. Then explain what is different about each character's personality or priorities that leads them to see the city so differently.
items.answer: Sofia's mother loves city life because of its energy, variety, and convenience. She grew up in a different way or simply enjoys stimulation. She sees the late-night buses and restaurants as exciting signs of life. Sofia feels overwhelmed. To her, the noise is not exciting, it is unsettling. She cannot sleep, which shows the city's pace is too much for her. Their different personalities are the key: the mother finds stimulation energizing, while Sofia finds it exhausting and disorienting.

steps: Mother's point of view: The city is exciting, diverse, and full of life and convenience.
Evidence: 'Restaurants open at midnight, buses running all night, people from everywhere!' — enthusiasm for variety.
Sofia's point of view: The city is overwhelming; the noise prevents rest and feels too fast.
Evidence: She cannot sleep and says 'everything is too loud and too fast.'
Mother's personality: She is energized by activity and change.
Sofia's personality: She is a quieter person who needs calm — the city overstimulates her.
Same place, same move, but completely different personal responses based on what each needs.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The town was debating whether to tear down an old, crumbling building and build a new park. Elder Rosa, who had lived in the neighborhood for sixty years, stood up at the meeting. "My mother got her first job in that building. It is part of who we are." A young parent, David, stood up next. "My kids need somewhere safe to play. History is wonderful, but you can't run through it."

Explain both Elder Rosa's and David's points of view. Use specific evidence. Then explain why the same building means something completely different to each person.
items.answer: Elder Rosa sees the old building as a living piece of community history. Her mother worked there, making it personally meaningful. To her, tearing it down erases the story of people who built the neighborhood. David sees an opportunity: a safe place for children to play. He respects history but believes children's present needs matter more than preserving a crumbling structure. The building means the past to Elder Rosa and wasted space to David. Both love their community, but they are measuring it at different points in time.

steps: Elder Rosa's point of view: The building has deep personal and community history — her mother worked there.
Evidence: 'It is part of who we are' — she sees the building as identity and memory.
David's point of view: A park would serve children's real, present needs.
Evidence: 'My kids need somewhere safe to play. History is wonderful, but you can't run through it.'
Why they differ: Elder Rosa is rooted in memory and what has been. David is focused on what his children need now.
Same building = irreplaceable history for one; obstacle to progress for the other.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Amara and her cousin Kofi both entered the school science fair. Amara's project won first place. Kofi's project did not place at all. Their grandmother hugged Amara and then turned to Kofi. "You worked just as hard. You'll win next time." Kofi pulled away. "Next time doesn't help right now," he said.

Explain Kofi's point of view and Grandmother's point of view. Why does Grandmother's comfort not help Kofi? Use evidence from the story.
items.answer: Grandmother is trying to comfort Kofi by looking ahead — she believes effort matters and the future holds another chance. Her intention is kind and encouraging. Kofi, however, is in the middle of his disappointment. 'Next time doesn't help right now' shows that he is not able to think about the future yet because the present hurt is too strong. Grandmother sees the big picture; Kofi is experiencing the immediate sting of loss. Her comfort, while well-meaning, does not meet Kofi where he is right now.

steps: Grandmother's point of view: Effort matters; losing once is not failure; the future brings new chances.
Evidence: 'You worked just as hard. You'll win next time' — forward-looking and affirming.
Kofi's point of view: The loss hurts right now, and future chances do not erase present disappointment.
Evidence: 'Next time doesn't help right now' — he cannot yet see past this moment.
Why the comfort doesn't help: Grandmother is thinking ahead; Kofi is still inside the painful moment.
Both care deeply, but they are in different emotional places at the same time.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Two students both read the same book about a wolf. Mia said, "The wolf is the villain. He tricked everyone." Her classmate Noah said, "I felt sorry for the wolf. Nobody in the story ever asked him why he acted that way."

Explain both Mia's and Noah's points of view about the wolf. What does each character pay attention to in the story? Why might two students reading the same book see the same character so differently?
items.answer: Mia's point of view is that the wolf is the villain because he tricked the other characters. She is focused on the wolf's actions and the harm he caused. Noah's point of view is more sympathetic. He notices that no one ever tried to understand the wolf's reasons. Noah is paying attention to what the story leaves out: the wolf's perspective. Two readers see the same character differently because Mia judges by what the wolf did, while Noah wonders about why he did it. Their different reading habits lead them to different conclusions.

steps: Mia's point of view: The wolf is a villain because he tricked people — she focuses on his harmful actions.
Evidence: 'He tricked everyone' — she sees the outcome of the wolf's behavior.
Noah's point of view: The wolf may have reasons that the story never explored — she focuses on what's missing.
Evidence: 'Nobody in the story ever asked him why he acted that way' — he is thinking about the wolf's inner life.
Mia focuses on actions; Noah focuses on motivation and empathy.
Both read the same story but ask different questions of it — one looks at what the wolf did, one wonders why.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

When the school added a uniform policy, Jade was upset. "My clothes are how I show who I am," she said. Her friend Tomás shrugged. "Now I don't have to think about what to wear every morning. That's one less thing to stress about."

Explain both Jade's and Tomás's points of view on the uniform policy. Then explain what each character's point of view tells you about what they value most.
items.answer: Jade's point of view is that the uniform policy takes away something important: the ability to express herself through her clothes. For her, clothing is part of her identity. Tomás's point of view is that the uniform actually helps him by removing a daily decision. He is relieved, not upset. What Jade values most is self-expression and individuality. What Tomás values most is simplicity and having fewer choices to make in the morning. The same policy removes freedom for one person and reduces stress for the other.

steps: Jade's point of view: Uniforms take away a form of self-expression she values deeply.
Evidence: 'My clothes are how I show who I am' — clothing is identity for her.
Tomás's point of view: Uniforms simplify his morning by removing a decision.
Evidence: 'One less thing to stress about' — he sees the change as practical relief.
Jade values self-expression; Tomás values simplicity and ease.
Same policy is a loss for one and a benefit for the other, depending on what each student values.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Elena's family raised chickens in the backyard. Their neighbor Mr. Webb complained to the city. "The noise and the smell are a problem for everyone on the block," he said at the neighborhood meeting. Elena's dad responded quietly, "My children learn where food comes from. They feed and care for living things every day. That's not nothing."

Explain Mr. Webb's and Elena's dad's points of view. Why does the same situation feel like a problem to one neighbor and a benefit to the other?
items.answer: Mr. Webb's point of view is that the chickens create noise and smells that affect the whole neighborhood. He sees a shared problem that nobody asked his permission to create. Elena's dad's point of view is that the chickens provide his children with an education in responsibility and where food comes from. To him, that is a significant benefit for his family. Mr. Webb measures the chickens by what they cost the neighborhood; Elena's dad measures them by what they give his children. The same backyard chickens are a nuisance to one and a learning opportunity to the other.

steps: Mr. Webb's point of view: The chickens create noise and smell that are unwanted in the shared neighborhood space.
Evidence: 'The noise and the smell are a problem for everyone on the block.'
Elena's dad's point of view: The chickens teach children about responsibility and food — a real educational benefit.
Evidence: 'My children learn where food comes from. They feed and care for living things every day.'
Mr. Webb measures the situation by what the neighborhood loses: quiet and clean air.
Elena's dad measures it by what his children gain: knowledge and responsibility.
Same chickens, but each person stands in a different relationship to them.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The library announced it was replacing many old books with e-books on tablets. The school librarian, Mr. Ahmed, was cautious. "Physical books don't need charging. Any student can use them, anytime, without technology." Second-grader Priya was thrilled. "You can carry a thousand books in one hand!"

Explain both Mr. Ahmed's and Priya's points of view about the library switching to e-books. What does each character know from experience that shapes their view?
items.answer: Mr. Ahmed is cautious because he knows that not all students have reliable access to technology at home. Physical books work for everyone without needing power or a device. His experience as a librarian serving all students makes him think about equity. Priya is excited because she sees the convenience: thousands of books in one device is amazing to her. She is thinking about access to more stories. Mr. Ahmed worries about who might be left out when technology is required. Priya focuses on how much more she could read. Both care about books, but they look at the change from different vantage points.

steps: Mr. Ahmed's point of view: Physical books are more equitable — they require no charging, no device, no access barriers.
Evidence: 'Any student can use them, anytime, without technology' — he is thinking about all students, including those without devices.
Priya's point of view: E-books are wonderfully convenient — you can have thousands of books in one place.
Evidence: 'You can carry a thousand books in one hand!' — she is excited by access to more content.
Mr. Ahmed's experience: He serves all kinds of students and knows not all have tech at home.
Priya's experience: She is a reader who wants more books and sees the upside of portability.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Nadia had been the top student in math for two years. This year, a new student named Theo joined the class. After the first test, Theo scored higher than Nadia. Their teacher, Ms. Lin, said to both of them, "Competition brings out the best in everyone." Nadia thought, "Easy for her to say — she's not the one who lost her spot."

Explain Ms. Lin's point of view and Nadia's point of view. Why does the teacher's comment land differently than she intends?
items.answer: Ms. Lin's point of view is positive and encouraging. She believes that having a strong competitor makes both students work harder and grow. Her comment is meant to motivate. Nadia's point of view is painful. She has held the top position for two years, and losing it feels personal. Ms. Lin has never been in that position herself, so her comment feels easy to say but hard to hear. Nadia's inner thought 'Easy for her to say — she's not the one who lost her spot' shows that the same event feels like growth to the teacher and like a loss to Nadia.

steps: Ms. Lin's point of view: Competition is good and helps everyone improve — her comment is encouraging and general.
Evidence: 'Competition brings out the best in everyone' — she believes this sincerely.
Nadia's point of view: The competition has taken away something she worked hard to earn — it feels like loss.
Evidence: 'Easy for her to say — she's not the one who lost her spot' — Nadia feels Ms. Lin can't understand.
Why the comment lands wrong: Ms. Lin is speaking from the outside; Nadia is living it from the inside.
Same event = growth for Ms. Lin's view; personal loss for Nadia's.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The town was having its first-ever multicultural food festival. Local baker Mrs. Chen was nervous. "I worry people won't try food that's unfamiliar to them," she said. Her teenage daughter Lin laughed. "Mom, people come to these things specifically to try new food. That's the whole point."

Explain Mrs. Chen's and Lin's points of view. What experiences or knowledge shapes each character's perspective?
items.answer: Mrs. Chen is nervous because she worries that people are reluctant to try unfamiliar food. Her experience as a baker who has seen customers stick to what they know makes her cautious. Lin is confident because she understands that people who attend a multicultural food festival are specifically looking for new experiences. Her knowledge of why people attend such events shapes her optimism. Mrs. Chen is thinking about general behavior; Lin is thinking about the specific people who would choose to come to this event.

steps: Mrs. Chen's point of view: People are often reluctant to try unfamiliar food, so the festival might not work.
Evidence: 'I worry people won't try food that's unfamiliar to them' — she focuses on the risk of rejection.
Lin's point of view: The festival's audience is self-selected — they came because they want new food.
Evidence: 'People come to these things specifically to try new food. That's the whole point.'
Mrs. Chen's experience: She has seen general customers avoid unfamiliar items.
Lin's knowledge: She understands the mindset of people who would choose to attend a cultural food event.
Both see the same festival, but through very different assumptions about what the audience wants.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Omar was chosen to speak at the school assembly. He practiced for two weeks. On the day of the speech, Omar's dad, who had immigrated from another country and still felt nervous speaking English in public, watched from the audience. After the speech, his dad's eyes were wet. "You did something I have never been able to do," his father told him.

Explain Omar's and his father's points of view on the same event. Why does the speech mean something different to each of them?
items.answer: To Omar, the speech is a performance he prepared for — it was nerve-wracking but also something his school asked him to do. To his father, Omar's speech represents something much bigger: his son is able to do publicly what the father cannot, speaking English confidently in front of a crowd. For his father, who still struggles with public English speaking as an immigrant, watching Omar means the sacrifice of immigration has led to his son's belonging and confidence. The same speech is a school event for Omar and a profound milestone for his father.

steps: Omar's point of view: The speech is a school task he worked hard to prepare for.
Evidence: 'He practiced for two weeks' — it was important and stressful, but a normal school activity.
Father's point of view: The speech represents something he himself has never been able to do.
Evidence: 'You did something I have never been able to do' — he is moved because Omar has surpassed a barrier the father still faces.
Father's experience: As an immigrant who feels nervous speaking English publicly, his son's ease is deeply meaningful.
Same event = school assignment for Omar; symbol of belonging and achievement for his father.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The old playground equipment was being replaced with new plastic equipment. Second-grader Isabel pointed at the new yellow slide and said, "It's so bright and shiny!" Her older brother, who was in fifth grade, crossed his arms. "That old wooden climbing structure was the best thing this school ever had. We practically grew up on it."

Explain Isabel's and her brother's points of view. Why does age and personal history lead them to see the same change differently?
items.answer: Isabel is excited because she sees new equipment that looks bright and fun. She does not have years of memories on the old equipment, so she only sees the new. Her older brother is upset because the old wooden structure was a big part of his childhood at this school. He has years of memories attached to it. Isabel sees what is being gained; her brother sees what is being lost. Their age and personal history with the old equipment lead to completely different emotional responses to the exact same change.

steps: Isabel's point of view: The new equipment is exciting and fresh — it looks bright and fun.
Evidence: 'It's so bright and shiny!' — she focuses on the appeal of the new.
Brother's point of view: The old wooden structure was irreplaceable — it holds years of memories.
Evidence: 'We practically grew up on it' — he sees the loss of something meaningful.
Isabel's history: She is young; she has few memories of the old equipment.
Brother's history: He has spent years on the old structure, making it emotionally significant.
Same change = fresh excitement for one; personal loss for the other.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

The whole class had to stay in for recess because a few students had misbehaved. Kenji, who was one of the students who had misbehaved, sat quietly and accepted the punishment. His classmate Yara, who had done nothing wrong, said to the teacher, "That's not fair. Why do I lose recess for what someone else did?"

Explain Kenji's and Yara's points of view on the group punishment. How does each character's role in the situation shape what they think is fair?
items.answer: Kenji accepts the punishment quietly. From his point of view, he was one of the students who misbehaved, so losing recess makes sense to him. He deserved a consequence. Yara's point of view is very different. She did nothing wrong and sees the group punishment as unfair. She is losing her recess for someone else's behavior, and that feels unjust. Kenji's role as someone who contributed to the problem makes the punishment feel earned. Yara's role as an innocent bystander makes the same punishment feel deeply unfair. Their different roles create completely different senses of justice.

steps: Kenji's point of view: He misbehaved, so the punishment is deserved — he accepts it.
Evidence: He 'sat quietly and accepted the punishment' — no protest, because he knows he contributed.
Yara's point of view: She did nothing wrong, so the group punishment is unjust.
Evidence: 'Why do I lose recess for what someone else did?' — she sees herself as unfairly caught in someone else's consequence.
Kenji's role: He is part of the cause — the punishment is logical from his perspective.
Yara's role: She is not part of the cause — the punishment feels arbitrary and unfair from her perspective.
Same consequence means justice to one and injustice to the other based on each person's role.

items.prompt:
Read the story below.

Auntie Bea had lived alone for thirty years. When Priya's family moved in nearby, they checked in on her every day. Auntie Bea told her friend, "They're always knocking on my door. I value my quiet." Priya told her mom, "I think Auntie Bea gets lonely. She always invites us in for tea."

Explain both Auntie Bea's and Priya's points of view. Then explain why the same visits mean something different to each character, and who you think may have a more complete picture of the situation.
items.answer: Auntie Bea's point of view, as she tells it to her friend, is that she values her quiet and the visits interrupt it. She has lived alone for thirty years and is used to her own schedule. Priya's point of view is that Auntie Bea is actually lonely, because she always invites them in for tea, which is an act of welcome. Priya may have a more complete picture because she is paying attention to what Auntie Bea does, not just what she says. Auntie Bea may say she wants quiet but act in a way that shows she enjoys the company. Both see the same visits, but Priya's observation of behavior gives her a window into what Auntie Bea's words do not fully reveal.

steps: Auntie Bea's point of view (stated): She values her quiet and the visits interrupt it.
Evidence: 'They're always knocking on my door. I value my quiet.'
Priya's point of view: Auntie Bea is lonely and actually welcomes the visits.
Evidence: 'She always invites us in for tea' — her actions show welcome, not rejection.
Why they differ: Auntie Bea describes what she tells herself; Priya observes what Auntie Bea actually does.
Who has the more complete picture: Priya, because she is paying attention to behavior as well as words.
This shows that point of view is not always what someone says — sometimes actions reveal more than words.
